bottom: Benson is the fundraising leader in an open seat race, with about $5.9 million cash on hand on August 24, 2026 against $1.5 million for James, and Benson and allied groups were booked to outspend James on television by roughly $23 million to $1 million heading into October, per AdImpact data reported by Bridge Michigan. Her money is broad and capped: Michigan limits gifts to $8,325 from individuals and $83,250 from PACs, so no single donor dominates her committee the way the DeVos family dominates the pro James super PAC. Four interests combine real money with a live decision on her desk.

**Data centers and the Saline Township project.** Her husband, Ryan Friedrichs, is a vice president of development at Related Companies, whose Related Digital is developing the $7 billion, 1.4 gigawatt OpenAI and Oracle data center in Saline Township. Related chairman Stephen Ross gave her the $8,325 maximum. She has pledged a statewide moratorium on new data centers. The MPSC data center tariff case and any moratorium bill land in 2027.

**Organized labor.** The UAW, SEIU and LIUNA each gave the $83,250 PAC maximum, and the UAW endorsed her on June 5, 2026. Building trades want the union construction jobs that data centers and state projects bring, which pulls against her moratorium pledge.

**Utilities.** Her campaign calls her the only candidate not taking utility money, yet her August filing shows $3,000 from DTE Energy executive chairman Gerardo Norcia. The next governor appoints the MPSC, and Proposal 2 on the November 3 ballot would ban utility political donations.

James's campaign is the smaller of the two, with $1.5 million on hand on August 24, 2026 against Benson's $5.9 million, and the RGA pulled nearly all its reserved ads in the final stretch, per Bridge Michigan on October 13, 2026. His real financial base is outside the capped campaign, in the Mission Michigan super PAC, where Dan and Pamella DeVos have given $6 million since 2025. Four interests pair money with a live decision.

**The DeVos family and school choice.** $6 million to Mission Michigan plus $112,575 from eleven family members and RDV Corp. employees to the campaign in 2026, with some gifts over the limit fixed by spousal attribution. James wants Michigan to opt into the federal Scholarship Tax Credit, a decision only the governor can make.

**Walbridge and the Rakolta family, builders of the Saline data center.** At least $113,850 to James committees since 2018. Walbridge is building the Saline Township data center that is the state's largest pending power decision. James backs local control and a moratorium while rules are written.

**Utilities.** DTE and Consumers Energy were the only two 2026 donors to Mission First People Always PAC, whose treasurer is a James congressional staffer and which passed most of the money to Republican party committees. Employees and utility PACs gave about $34,000 more across his accounts. The next governor appoints the MPSC.

D.t: Jocelyn Benson leads by 12.5 in the forecast and wins 99% of simulations. The cushion is about 619,126 votes; a one point swing is about 24,845 voters changing sides.
In 8 of 10 simulations the result lands between D +5.8 and D +19.2. Only an unusual polling error changes the winner.
The polls page average is D +8.0. Your best recent poll is Suffolk University at D +15.4; your worst is YouGov at D +2.2. 16 polls in the last 30 days.

The biggest vote banks for Democrats: Wayne, a projected net 369,597 votes; Oakland, a projected net 179,467 votes; Washtenaw, a projected net 118,601 votes. Every point of extra turnout here is worth more than persuasion anywhere else.
The large counties within 12 points: Macomb, D +2.8, 8.7% of the vote; Saginaw, D +5.9, 1.8% of the vote; Muskegon, D +11.9, 1.7% of the vote; Berrien, D +2.5, 1.5% of the vote.

D.h: Where you run behind the 2024 map
D.t: Against the 2024 presidential vote, Jocelyn Benson runs furthest behind in Ottawa, Saginaw, Berrien. That is where the forecast sees voters who backed your side two years ago and have not come back yet.

Groups big enough to move the race: White voters, 82% of voters, 50 to 48, where a 5 point gain is worth 4.12 points; Voters who cast ballots in 2022 and 2024, 75% of voters, 54 to 43, where a 5 point gain is worth 3.75 points; Voters without a degree, 63% of voters, 53 to 44, where a 5 point gain is worth 3.15 points.

The forecast's worst groups for Jocelyn Benson: Immigration voters 22 to 76, Small counties 37 to 60, Voters who can afford daily costs 44 to 53. Cutting the loss here is often cheaper than winning new groups.
$5.9M cash against $1.5M. Spend it early on persuasion television in the battleground counties and keep a reserve for the last week.
